name: Nyx
note: The children of Night, who have a mother and no father

Moros.name: Moros (Fatum)
Moros.note: Doom -- not death but the appointed end a man walks toward. Roman: Fatum, whence fate, fatal. Theog. 211

Thanatos.name: Thanatos (Mors)
Thanatos.note: Death himself, with a heart of iron and no pity; the only god who takes no gifts. Roman: Mors. Gives euthanasia, thanatology, and Freud's thanatos. Theog. 212, 763-766

Hypnos.name: Hypnos (Somnus)
Hypnos.note: Sleep, twin of Death and gentler; he lives with him but walks the earth kindly. Roman: Somnus, whence somnolent, insomnia. From the Greek: hypnosis, hypnotic. Theog. 212, 758-762

Nemesis.name: Nemesis (Invidia)
Nemesis.note: Retribution -- the pang that visits a man who has too much and forgets it. Roman: Invidia. The English word is unchanged and needs no translation, which is rare. Theog. 223

Eris.name: Eris (Discordia)
Eris.note: Strife, who threw the golden apple among the goddesses and started the Trojan War with it. Roman: Discordia, whence discord. Gives eristic, the art of wrangling. Theog. 225

Geras.name: Geras (Senectus)
Geras.note: Old age, counted among the evils. Roman: Senectus. Gives geriatric, gerontology. Theog. 225

Momos.name: Momos (Querella)
Momos.note: Blame, mockery, the fault-finder; thrown out of heaven for criticising the gods' work. Gives momus, a carping critic. Theog. 214

Apate.name: Apate (Fraus)
Apate.note: Deceit. Roman: Fraus, whence fraud. Theog. 224

Philotes.name: Philotes (Amicitia)
Philotes.note: Affection, and the act of love. Roman: Amicitia. The root phil- is everywhere in English: philosophy, philanthropy, bibliophile. Theog. 224

Ker.name: Ker (Letum)
Ker.note: Violent death, as against Thanatos' quiet one -- the fate that catches a man on the battlefield. Theog. 211

Moirai.name: Moirai (Parcae)
Moirai.note: The three Fates counted as one record because they act as one: Klotho spins the thread, Lachesis measures it, Atropos -- the unturnable -- cuts it. Roman: Parcae (Nona, Decuma, Morta). Hesiod gives them twice, once to Nyx alone and once to Zeus and Themis; both readings are old and the tree draws the first. Gives atropine, from Atropos, because the deadly nightshade kills. Theog. 217-222, 904-906

Hesperides.note: The daughters of Evening, who keep the golden apples at the western edge of the world -- Herakles' eleventh labour. Hesperus, the evening star, is the same word; Hesperia was a Roman name for Italy, the land toward sunset. Theog. 215-216

Oneiroi.note: The tribe of Dreams. Ovid names three of them, of whom Morpheus -- the shaper, who takes human form in a sleeper's dream -- gives English morphine, named in 1805 for the sleep it brings. Theog. 212; Ov. Met. 11.633-643

Lethe.note: Forgetfulness, and the river of it in the underworld, from which the dead drink. Gives lethal, lethargy, and 'alethia', the Greek for truth, which is literally un-forgetting. Theog. 227

Algea.note: Pains. Gives analgesic, neuralgia, nostalgia -- the ache for return. Theog. 227

Dysnomia.note: Lawlessness. The moon of the dwarf planet Eris is named for her. Theog. 230

Ate.note: Ruin: the blindness sent on a man before his fall, the delusion that makes him do the thing that destroys him. Theog. 230

Horkos.note: Oath, the most dangerous of them, who punishes any man who swears falsely. Theog. 231-232

Makhai.note: Battles. Gives -machy: logomachy, a war of words. Theog. 228

unions.note: Night bore all of these lying with none: a virgin birth of fourteen, and the tree's only union of that size. Theog. 211-225
Hateful Strife bore them all alone. Theog. 226-232
